summary:
Our team tackled the "Abandoned, but Not Forgotten" challenge by developing an interactive digital atlas of human artifacts left in space. Because every extra kilogram drastically increases ascent fuel consumption, astronauts had to leave equipment behind to maximize the return of research samples.

The platform switches between isolated Lunar and Martian models, featuring high-resolution satellite photomosaics pinned with real landing sites. Each artifact includes a detailed dossier with exact coordinates sourced from the NASA History Program Office, NSSDC Master Catalog, and Apollo Lunar Surface Journal—covering both mission hardware and personal mementos like golf balls, medals, a Bible, and a family photo.

Users can assess structural wear over time via the Condition & Degradation slider, inspect the mass breakdown of aluminum, titanium, and microelectronics in the Material tab, and send components to the Recycle calculator to estimate their manufacturing potential for NASA’s space-debris recycling goals. The site also features an interactive laser retroreflector simulation demonstrating Earth-to-Moon distance calculations alongside all official data sources in the footer.
details:
Option 1: Structured by Question (for detailed project description)

What it does & How it works: Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is an interactive dual-world web archive that documents human-made hardware left on the Moon (~187,400 kg, or the weight of 22 elephants)and Mars. Users can switch between isolated Lunar and Martian environments, explore exact landing and impact coordinates on a 2D Leaflet surface atlas and a 3D WebGL planetary globe, read 4-tab mission dossiers (Surveyor, Lunar Orbiter, Apollo 11–17, Saturn V S-IVB, Viking 1, Pathfinder & Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, and Ingenuity), test an Earth-to-Moon laser retroreflector simulation, and estimate recoverable alloys with an In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) recycling calculator.

Benefits & Intended Impact: The project turns dense technical records—such as the 22-page NASA History Program Office catalogueand NSSDC mission logs—into an accessible visual field guide. Its goal is to reshape how people view discarded spacecraft: not as "space debris," but as both irreplaceable archaeological monuments and a practical metal reserve for future off-world bases.

Tools, Languages & Software: Developed in Visual Studio Code using HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS, and Vanilla JavaScript with a modular, data-driven architecture (index.html, app.js, data.js). We integrated Leaflet.js with NASA LROC and MOLA global basemaps for 2D cartography, Three.js (WebGL) for interactive 3D globes, and custom spring-physics motion for the Hero planet view.

Creativity: We combined a clean, editorial NASA-inspired UI with interactive storytelling mechanics: a Surface Exposure Timeline Slider (Landing Day → Present Day → +100 Years in Vacuum), a visual Laser Ranging Signal Lab demonstrating the Moon's 3.8 cm/year orbital recession, and a Human Trace Gallery showcasing personal astronauts' keepsakes (Gagarin and Komarov medals, two golf balls, a falcon feather, and Charles Duke’s family photo).

Factors Considered: Our team prioritized documentary accuracy and ethical balance: strictly isolating Lunar and Martian datasets, separating non-Mars missions (Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10, Kepler) into a dedicated Beyond Mars context block, refusing to invent material mass breakdowns where official NASA summaries lacked verified figures, and weighing historical preservation against future resource recycling.

Option 2: Short Combined Version (Single paragraph for strict character limits)

Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is an interactive web archive that transforms NASA’s Catalogue of Manmade Material on the Moon (~187,400 kg of hardware)and Mars mission records into an accessible 2D/3D digital museum. Built with HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS, Vanilla JavaScript, Leaflet.js (NASA LROC/MOLA basemaps), and Three.js (WebGL), the platform lets users switch between isolated Moon and Mars views, inspect landing sites on a 2D map and 3D globe, and explore 4-tab mission dossiers. Its creativity lies in blending archival storytelling with interactive tools: a surface degradation timeline slider, a visual Apollo laser retroreflector lab (illustrating the Moon’s 3.8 cm/year drift), a gallery of personal astronaut keepsakes, and an ISRU metal-recycling calculator. Our team considered strict factual integrity—avoiding unverified mass estimates, distinguishing surface hardware from deep-space missions, and highlighting the balance between preserving space heritage and recycling orbital-class metals for future exploration.
